t: 欢迎使用 TraceDraw 帮助
h: 本帮助的组织方式 在 TraceDraw 中获取帮助 从哪里开始
x: 欢迎使用 TraceDraw 帮助 TraceDraw 是一款免费的开源矢量绘图程序。你可以用它绘制插画、标志、图表、版面和印刷品，它们由在任何尺寸下都保持清晰的形状、线条和文字组成，还可以与位图结合。同一个程序可在 Windows、macOS 和 Linux 以及网页浏览器中运行。 本帮助一步步说明如何在 TraceDraw 中完成工作，以及每个对话框、面板和工具的作用。 本帮助的组织方式 左侧的目录按照工作的顺序排列： 入门 介绍工作区、新建绘图、打开和保存。 线条、形状和轮廓、对象、符号和图层 以及 颜色、填充和透明度 介绍绘制和排列对象。 特殊效果、文本、模板和样式、页面和版面 以及 位图 涵盖其余的绘图工作。 打印、网页图形 和 文件格式 介绍如何把作品从 TraceDraw 输出。 自定义和自动化 介绍选项、工作区、脚本和 AI 功能，参考 列出每个菜单命令、工具、面板和键盘快捷键。 使用 搜索 选项卡可按页面中的任意字词查找页面，使用顶部的语言列表可用另一种语言阅读同一页面。 在 TraceDraw 中获取帮助 按 F1 打开眼前内容的页面：打开的对话框，否则是显示的面板，再否则是当前工具。 单击对话框或选项页底部的 ? 按钮，打开它的页面。 选择 帮助 > 帮助主题 打开本页。 提示 面板会在你工作时说明当前工具；其中的 了解更多 链接会打开该工具在这里的页面。请参阅 提示。 页面会在网页浏览器中以 TraceDraw 设置的语言打开。 从哪里开始 如果你刚开始使用 TraceDraw，请先阅读 工作区，然后阅读 创建绘图 和 绘制线条和曲线。

s: 欢迎使用 TraceDraw 帮助
h: 在程序中查看新内容 最近版本的亮点
x: 新增功能 TraceDraw 的每个版本都会增加功能和修复。本页介绍如何了解更改内容，并列出最近版本的亮点。 在程序中查看新内容 选择 帮助 > 新增功能 打开欢迎屏幕的新增功能页面，其中有本版本的新闻。 打开 帮助 > 突出显示新增功能，在菜单中标出本版本的新内容：每个新命令的末尾、通向新命令的子菜单箭头旁，以及包含新命令的菜单标题上方都会出现一个小圆点。关闭该命令后标记消失，下次启动 TraceDraw 时该命令又会关闭。 每个版本的完整更改列表在项目的 更改日志 中。 最近版本的亮点 使用你的语言的帮助。 每个 ? 按钮和 F1 都会以 TraceDraw 设置的语言打开本帮助中关于眼前对话框、面板或工具的页面。 文档属性。 文件 > 文档属性 保存绘图的语言、标题、主题、作者、版权、标签、备注和评分，并附有绘图内容的完整报告。请参阅 文档属性。 颜色管理。 工具 > 颜色管理 设置绘图的配置文件和新绘图的默认值，并为打开或导入的文件设定策略。请参阅 颜色管理。 条形码和二维码。 三步向导可放置条形码，二维码则是可在 属性 面板中编辑的动态对象。请参阅 条形码和二维码。 效果。 效果 菜单集中了各效果面板；调和可以按固定间距沿路径排列，并按顺时针或逆时针旋转颜色。请参阅 调和。 路径文本 有自己的方向、位置、距离和偏移设置。请参阅 添加和编辑文本。 字体管理器 整理已安装的字体、文件夹、收藏和集合。请参阅 字体和字形。

s: 欢迎使用 TraceDraw 帮助
h: 关于对话框 检查更新 自动检查 欢迎屏幕 社区和支持
x: 关于 TraceDraw 和更新 TraceDraw 免费且开源。本页介绍如何查看你的版本、如何获取更新的版本，以及在哪里寻求帮助。 关于对话框 选择 帮助 > 关于 TraceDraw 可查看正在运行的版本、作者、许可证、源代码链接以及程序的构成。按 关闭、Enter 或 Esc 关闭。  检查更新 在桌面版中，TraceDraw 可以在新版本发布时通知你。 立即检查： 选择 帮助 > 更新。 TraceDraw 向项目的发布页面查询最新版本，并说明它是否比你的版本新。测试版本和每夜构建从不提供。 有更新的版本时，选择要做的操作： 下载 打开适用于你系统的文件下载（Windows 上为安装程序或便携压缩包， Mac 上为适合其处理器的磁盘映像，Linux 上为 AppImage 或压缩包）。之后由系统的安装程序完成安装。 发行说明 打开该版本的更改列表。 跳过此版本 不再提供该版本。 关闭 关闭对话框。 当 TraceDraw 以 Linux AppImage 运行时，对话框还可能提供 安装：它把新的 AppImage 下载到正在运行的文件旁边，检查下载是否完整且真实，然后替换旧文件。新版本会在你下次打开 TraceDraw 时启动。如果有任何检查不通过，旧文件保持原样，对话框会告诉你原因。 如果检查失败（例如没有网络连接），对话框会说明并提供发布页面。  自动检查 工具 > 选项 > 全局 的 常规 页面有一个在启动时检查更新的设置。它默认开启：TraceDraw 每天在启动时静默检查一次，只有在出现你未跳过的新版本时才提示。 TraceDraw 首次启动时会询问是否检查更新：始终检查 或 从不检查。在您回答之前，TraceDraw 不会自行建立任何连接。您的回答会设置此选项，之后可随时在此处更改。 注意： 浏览器版本始终是最新的。在浏览器版本中， 帮助 > 更新 会打开发布页面。 欢迎屏幕 欢迎屏幕是 TraceDraw 启动时的第一个选项卡。你可以在这里新建绘图、打开最近使用的绘图（每个都带缩略图；清除列表 会清除它们）、从模板开始、阅读新闻和查找学习资料。选择 帮助 > 欢迎屏幕 可再次显示它。帮助 > 视频教程、 快速入门指南 和 用户指南 打开它的学习页面， 新增功能 打开它的新闻。 社区和支持 帮助 > 社区 打开项目的讨论论坛，你可以在那里提问和分享想法。 帮助 > 支持 打开问题跟踪器，你可以在那里报告问题。 帮助 > 消息设置 打开设置 TraceDraw 消息的选项。
入门 这些页面介绍 TraceDraw：窗口的各个部分，如何新建、打开和保存绘图，如何在绘图中移动和撤消操作，以及绘图时在哪里获得帮助。 TraceDraw 可在 Windows、macOS 和 Linux 上运行，也可以不安装任何东西就在网页浏览器中运行。两者是同一个程序；浏览器版本的少数差异在 浏览器版本 中说明。

h: The parts of the window The standard toolbar The property bar The toolbox and flyouts Panels The drawing window The color palette The status bar Arranging the bars Working with several drawings The interface size
x: The workspace The TraceDraw window holds your drawings and everything you need to work on them. This page names its parts, so the other pages of this Help make sense. The parts of the window From top to bottom and from left to right: The menu bar holds every command, in the menus File, Edit, View, Layout, Object, Effects, Bitmaps, Text, Table, Tools, Window and Help. Each command shows its shortcut beside it. With no drawing open, only File, Tools, Window and Help are shown. The Menu commands page lists every command. The standard toolbar holds the common commands (see below). The property bar shows the settings of what you are doing now. The document tabs show one tab per open drawing. The toolbox, on the left, holds the tools. The rulers run along the top and the left of the drawing window. The drawing window shows the page on the desktop around it. The panels sit on the right. The color palette runs along the bottom. The status bar, at the very bottom, describes the active tool and the selection. The standard toolbar The standard toolbar holds, in groups: New, Open (its arrow lists the drawings you used last), Save and Print. Cut, Copy and Paste. Undo and Redo. Their arrows list the steps, so you can undo or redo several at once by choosing a step. Import, Export and Publish to PDF. The zoom box: type a zoom level and press Enter, or open its list for zoom to selected, to all objects, to the page, to the page width or height, and levels from 10% to 1600%. Then full-screen preview. Show rulers, show grid and show guidelines, drawn pressed while on. Snap off (Alt+Q) and the list of what to snap to. Options, which opens the list of option pages. Launch: Font Manager, Welcome Screen and Color Management. Hover a button to see its name, its shortcut and what it does. The property bar The property bar changes with what you do. With nothing selected and the Pick tool active, it shows the page size and orientation, the drawing units and the nudge distance. With objects selected, it shows their position, size, scale, rotation and mirror buttons, then the settings of that kind of object. Each tool adds its own settings, explained on the page of the tool. In number fields you can type a sum such as 10+5, or a value in another unit such as 1 in, which is converted to the drawing units. The toolbox and flyouts The toolbox has one button per group of tools. A button with a small arrow at its corner holds a flyout, a list of related tools. To open a flyout, click the arrow, right-click the button, or press and hold it. The button then shows the tool you used last from that group. Hover a tool to see its name, its shortcut and what it does. Double-clicking some buttons has a shortcut action: Pick selects all objects, Zoom zooms to fit all objects and Rectangle adds a rectangle the size of the page. The + button at the end of the toolbox lists the groups with a check box to show or hide each one, and resets the toolbox. The Toolbox page lists every tool. Panels Panels hold settings you keep open while you work, such as Properties, Objects and Hints, which are open at first. Open panels are tabs down the right side; click a tab to bring its panel to the front, or click the tab in front to fold the panels away. Open other panels from Window > Panels or with their shortcuts; the + under the tabs adds one. Each panel has collapse and close buttons in its title bar. The Panels page lists every panel. The drawing window The page sits on the desktop, the area around it, where you can also keep objects. Below the drawing are: the page navigator: insert a page before, first page, previous page, the page number, next page, last page and insert a page after; one tab per page (click to go to a page, double-click to rename it); the horizontal scroll bar. Drag the dotted splitter between the page tabs and the scroll bar to share the space between them. The Navigator button in the corner between the scroll bars shows a thumbnail of the page while you hold it; move the pointer over the thumbnail to move the view. Double-clicking the page border with the Pick tool opens the page size options. The color palette Click a color of the palette to fill the selected objects; right-click it to color their outline. The document palette under the drawing window collects the colors your drawing uses. See Color palettes. The status bar The status bar shows a hint for the active tool, what is selected and on which layer, and the fill and outline of the selection. Double-click the fill or outline part to change them. The Status bar page explains each part. Arranging the bars You can move the toolbox, the color palette, the standard toolbar, the property bar and the status bar: drag a bar by its dotted grip to another edge of the window, or away from the edges to make it float. Right-click a grip to lock the bars or reset their positions. To show or hide a bar, use Window > Toolbars. You can also save the whole arrangement as a workspace; see Workspaces. Working with several drawings Each open drawing has its own tab above the rulers, with its name and a * while it has unsaved changes. The tab after the last one creates a new drawing. Each drawing keeps its own pages, undo history, selection, zoom and units. Window > Cascade, Tile Horizontally and Tile Vertically show every drawing in a window of its own; Combine Windows brings the tabs back. New Window opens a second window of the same drawing, for example to see two pages or two zoom levels at once; an edit in one window shows in all of them. The interface size If menus and buttons look too small or too large, choose Tools > Options > Customization and set the interface size on the Appearance page. The interface size never changes the size of your drawing. See Customization options.

h: To create a drawing General Dimensions Color settings Skipping the dialog box Other ways to start
x: Creating a drawing Every drawing starts with a page size, a number of pages, a color mode and a resolution. You choose them in the Create a New Document dialog box. To create a drawing Choose File > New (Ctrl+N), click New on the standard toolbar, click the + after the last document tab, or click New Document on the Welcome Screen. In the Create a New Document dialog box, set the values described below. Click OK or press Enter. The drawing opens in its own tab. The dialog box remembers your values for the next drawing.  General Name names the drawing. It starts as the next Untitled-N. Preset sets the color mode, page size, units and resolution at once. The presets are TraceDraw default and Default CMYK (CMYK, A4, millimeters, 300 dpi), Default RGB (RGB, A4, millimeters, 300 dpi) and Web (RGB, 1920 x 1080 pixels, 72 dpi). When you change one of those values, the preset shows Custom unless the values match a preset again. The button beside the preset holds Save Preset, which asks for a Preset name and adds the current values to the list, and Delete Preset, which removes a preset you saved. The built-in presets cannot be deleted. Number of pages sets how many pages the drawing has, from 1 to 999. Each page is named "Page N" and has one layer. Primary color mode is CMYK, for print, or RGB, for screens. Dimensions Page size lists the paper sizes, or Custom. Choosing a size keeps the current orientation. A width and height you type that match a paper size, in either orientation, select its name. Width and Height set the page size, in the units you choose in the list beside the width. Those units become the drawing units of the property bar. Orientation: Portrait or Landscape. Resolution in dpi (300 at first). It is used for the effects that are turned into pixels, and to measure sizes in pixels: 1920 pixels are 162.56 mm at 300 dpi and 677.33 mm at 72 dpi. When the units are pixels, changing the resolution keeps the page's size in pixels. Color settings Open Color settings to choose the RGB profile, CMYK profile and Grayscale profile of the drawing and the Rendering intent. They start at sRGB, the built-in CMYK profile, a 20% dot gain grayscale and relative colorimetric. See Color management. Skipping the dialog box Tick Do not show this dialog again to create new drawings at once, with the values you used last. To see the dialog box again, turn on the matching setting on the General page of Tools > Options > TraceDraw. See TraceDraw options. Other ways to start File > New from Template starts from a template. See Templates. File > Open opens an existing drawing. See Opening and saving drawings.

h: Opening a drawing Notes after opening Saving a drawing Save As Closing drawings Auto-backup and recovery
x: Opening and saving drawings TraceDraw saves drawings in its own format, .tdraw, which keeps everything, and can also save .cdr files. It opens many other formats; see Supported file formats. Opening a drawing Choose File > Open (Ctrl+O), or click Open on the standard toolbar. Choose the file and confirm. The drawing opens in a new tab. To open a drawing you used recently, use File > Open Recent, the arrow of the Open button, or the list on the Welcome Screen; Clear list empties the list. File > Import (Ctrl+I) instead adds the content of a file to the drawing that is open; see Importing files. Notes after opening When some objects of an opened file could not be read, or the drawing uses fonts that are not installed on your computer, a message says so after the file opens: For objects that could not be read, it gives their number. A Report button opens a new issue for the file on the project's issue tracker, so the problem can be fixed. For missing fonts, it names them. The text shows in a similar font and keeps its font name, so it comes back as it was on a computer that has the font. Tick Do not show this message again to stop these messages. You can turn them on again on the Warnings page of Tools > Options > Global. Saving a drawing Choose File > Save (Ctrl+S) to write the drawing back to its file. A new drawing, or one opened from a format TraceDraw only reads, has no file yet, so Save opens the Save Drawing dialog box. Save As File > Save As (Ctrl+Shift+S) saves the drawing under another name, in another folder or in another format.  To save a drawing under a new name: Choose the folder. The list on the left has shortcuts to Home, Desktop, Documents, Downloads and Pictures, and to the drives. Up one level goes to the folder above; you can also type a folder in the path bar and press Enter. New folder makes a folder and opens it. Double-click a folder of the list to open it; click a file to take its name. Type the File name. The extension of the chosen type is added. Choose Save as type: TraceDraw (*.tdraw) or CDR files (*.cdr). Choose the Version. For TraceDraw files it is the version of the format, newest first. For .cdr files it is the version of the file, from 27 down to 14; an older program can only open a version as old as itself or older. The version you choose stays with the drawing, so Save writes it again without asking. For .cdr files from version 16, Embed colour profile stores the drawing's CMYK profile in the file, and Embed fonts stores the fonts the text uses when their license allows it. Both choices are kept for the next time. Optionally fill in Title, Subject and a Rating (click the lit last star again to take it off). They are the drawing's properties, also shown in Document properties. Click Save or press Enter. If the file exists, TraceDraw asks whether to Replace it. The dialog box starts in the drawing's folder, else in the folder you saved to last, else in your documents folder. Note: In the browser version every save is a download: the dialog box keeps the name, type, version and properties, and the browser puts the file in its downloads folder. Other ways to save: File > Save as Template saves a template (see Templates), Export writes other formats (see Exporting), Publish to PDF writes a PDF (see Publishing to PDF), Send To saves a PDF to your desktop or documents folder or attaches it to an email, and GitHub keeps drawings in a GitHub repository (see GitHub). Revert goes back to the version last saved. Closing drawings Choose File > Close (Ctrl+F4), click the close button on the drawing's tab, or middle-click the tab. Close All closes every drawing, and Exit (Alt+F4) closes TraceDraw. When a drawing has unsaved changes, TraceDraw asks whether to save them first: Yes saves (asking for a name if the drawing has no file yet), No closes without saving, and Cancel keeps the drawing open. When several drawings have changes, it asks about each one; Cancel stops.  Auto-backup and recovery On the desktop, TraceDraw keeps backups of your open drawings while auto-backup is on (the Save page of Tools > Options > TraceDraw sets how often and where; every 20 minutes at first). Closing TraceDraw normally removes them. If TraceDraw ended without closing, for example after a power cut, it offers the backups the next time it starts: Recover opens each one as an unsaved drawing (Save then asks where to save it), and Discard leaves the backups in their folder. Two TraceDraw windows running at once never offer each other's drawings.

h: Undoing and redoing The Undo panel Zooming The Zoom tool Panning Views
x: Undoing, zooming and panning You can undo any change, and look at your drawing at any zoom level and from any position. Zooming and panning never change the drawing. Undoing and redoing Edit > Undo (Ctrl+Z) takes back the last change; Redo (Ctrl+Shift+Z) does it again. The arrows beside Undo and Redo on the standard toolbar list the steps. Choose a step to undo or redo every change up to it. Repeat applies the last command again, for example to the next object you select. The Undo panel The Undo panel lists every change of the drawing, oldest first. Click a step to take the drawing back to how it was after that step; click a later step to go forward again. Open it from Window > Panels.  Zooming Turn the mouse wheel to zoom in or out about the pointer. Use the zoom box on the standard toolbar: type a level, or choose one from its list (10% to 1600%), or zoom to the selection, all objects, the page, the page width or the page height. View > Zoom In and Zoom Out zoom one step; Zoom To Fit (F4) shows all objects, Zoom To Page (Shift+F4) the page and Zoom To Selected (Shift+F2) the selection. A trackpad pinch zooms, and on a touch screen two fingers pan and pinch with any tool. The Zoom tool Choose the Zoom tool (Z or F2), then: click to zoom in by two at that point; Shift+click or right-click to zoom out by two; drag a rectangle to zoom so the rectangle fills the window. With F2 the tool zooms once: after the click or the rectangle, the tool you had before comes back. With Z it stays until you choose another tool. Double-click the tool's button to zoom to fit all objects. Panning Hold the middle mouse button and drag, with any tool. Choose the Pan tool (H) and drag. Ctrl+wheel scrolls up and down, Alt+wheel sideways. Use the scroll bars, which cover the page and one page size around it. Hold the Navigator button in the corner between the scroll bars and move the pointer over the thumbnail of the page. PgUp and PgDn go to the previous and next page. To make the wheel scroll instead of zoom, change the mouse wheel action on the Zoom/Pan page of Tools > Options > Tools. Then the wheel scrolls, Shift+wheel scrolls sideways and Ctrl+wheel zooms. See Tool options. Views The View menu chooses how objects are drawn: Wireframe shows outlines only, Normal and Enhanced draw fills and effects, and Pixels shows the drawing as the pixels of an export. Full-screen Preview shows the page alone on the screen; press any key to come back. Preview Selected Only limits that preview to the selection. The View menu also shows or hides the rulers, grids, guidelines, bleed and printable area; see Rulers, grids and guidelines.

h: What the panel shows Moving between pages
x: The Hints panel The Hints panel explains the tool you are using, while you use it. It is open at first, beside Properties and Objects; open it again with Help > Hints or from Window > Panels.  What the panel shows The home page introduces the panel and lists topics such as drawing lines, shapes, selecting, moving and rotating objects, effects, outlines, fills, text, AI and getting help. Each topic is a link. A topic page explains the topic and lists the tools that serve it, each with its icon, its name and what it does. Click a tool to see its page. A tool page tells you how to use the tool, one instruction per line with the keys in bold, and links to the topic that lists the tool. Every page ends with Learn more, a link to the page of this Help that explains the tool or topic in full. Moving between pages When you choose another tool, the panel shows that tool's page. The bar at the bottom of the panel has Home on the left and Back and forward on the right, like a web browser.

h: The message at start What differs from the desktop
x: The browser version You can use TraceDraw in a web browser with nothing to install. It is the same program as the desktop version, built for the browser, so the menus, tools and files are the same.  The message at start Each time the page opens, a message explains that the browser version is the same program as the desktop one, and what differs. OK (or Enter) closes it; a second button opens the downloads of the desktop version. What differs from the desktop Speed. Large drawings, heavy effects, tracing, mosaics and big exports are slower, and keep the page busy until they finish. The desktop version runs at full speed. Files. Opening and importing use the browser's file picker; saving, exporting and printing download a file. Recent drawings are not listed, because a browser cannot reopen an uploaded file. Fonts. The page brings its own fonts and fetches more the first time your text needs them. Settings are kept in that browser on that computer. Keys. While the drawing has the focus, the program's shortcuts reach TraceDraw instead of the browser, except the clipboard keys, reload and the browser's developer tools. Ctrl+N, Ctrl+T and Ctrl+W always stay with the browser, so use the File menu to create and close drawings. Screens. It suits a desktop browser with a mouse and keyboard. On a tablet, use the Touch workspace (see Workspaces); a phone screen is too small for editing. Macros. Macro projects load and run in the desktop version only. In the browser, every macro command shows a message saying so, with a button to the desktop downloads. Updates. The browser version is always the latest; there is nothing to install. Auto-backup and session recovery are desktop features.

h: Before you start: the token Opening a drawing from GitHub Saving a drawing to GitHub When GitHub refuses a save Opening an earlier version
x: Keeping drawings on GitHub TraceDraw can open drawings from a GitHub repository and save them back as commits, on the desktop and in the browser. Each save becomes a version in the repository's history, which you can open again later. The commands are in File > GitHub. Before you start: the token Public repositories open without a token. To open private ones and to save, create a fine-grained personal access token on GitHub with read and write access to the contents of the repository, and paste it in the Token field. The token is kept while TraceDraw runs. Tick Remember the token on this computer to keep it for the next time; it is then stored in plain text in your preferences (in the browser, in that browser's storage). The dialog boxes also remember the last repository, branch and path. Opening a drawing from GitHub Choose File > GitHub > Open from GitHub. Type the Repository as owner/name or its github.com address. Type the Branch, or leave it empty for main. Type the path of the File in the repository, for example art/logo.tdraw. Click OK. The drawing opens in a new tab, named after the file. It remembers where it came from and which version it was.  Saving a drawing to GitHub For a drawing opened from GitHub, Save (Ctrl+S) saves it back. For any drawing, choose File > GitHub > Save to GitHub. Check the repository, branch and path. Write a Commit message that says what changed (it starts as "Update" and the file name). Click OK. The drawing is saved as a .tdraw file, with its fonts, as a new commit on that branch. Save As still saves a file on your computer.  When GitHub refuses a save If the file changed on GitHub since you opened it, or a file already exists at that path and your drawing did not come from it, GitHub refuses the save and the dialog box says so. Save under another path or branch, or open the newer version first. The dialog box also explains other problems: a token that is refused or has no access, too many requests, a repository, branch or file that does not exist, a path that is a folder, a file that is not a drawing, or a drawing larger than 100 MB. Opening an earlier version For a drawing opened from GitHub, choose File > GitHub > History. The box lists the commits that changed the file, newest first, with their short id, date, author and message. Select one and click Open: that version opens as a new drawing, named after the file and the commit, which is not tied to GitHub.
线条、形状和轮廓 你在 TraceDraw 中绘制的一切都由线条和形状组成。这些页面介绍绘制它们的工具、如何逐个节点地改变形状、如何组合和切割它们，以及如何设置绘制其边缘的轮廓。 线条和曲线用曲线展开工具栏中的工具绘制，矩形、椭圆、多边形和其他形状用各自的工具绘制。任何对象绘制后都可以用 形状 工具改变形状。

h: Freehand 2-Point Line Bezier Pen B-Spline Polyline 3-Point Curve Continuing a curve The property bar Editing curves afterwards
x: Drawing lines and curves A line in TraceDraw is a curve: a path made of segments that join at nodes. Segments can be straight or curved. A curve can be open, with two ends, or closed, when its end meets its start, and then it can be filled. The curve tools are in the Curve flyout of the toolbox. Every one of them draws a curve with the default fill and outline of new objects; change them afterwards in the Properties panel or with the color palette. Freehand The Freehand tool (F5) draws a line where you drag, like a pencil. Choose the Freehand tool. Drag on the page. Release the button to finish. TraceDraw follows the pointer and smooths the line when you release it. The smoothing (0 to 100, 50 at first) on the property bar sets how much: a higher value gives fewer nodes and a softer line. When you are zoomed in, the line keeps more detail. To draw a straight line with this tool, click where the line starts and click again where it ends. Hold Ctrl to keep the line to steps of 15 degrees. Esc drops the first click. 2-Point Line The 2-Point Line tool draws one straight segment: press where it starts and release where it ends, or click twice. Hold Ctrl to keep it to steps of 15 degrees. Bezier The Bezier tool draws precise curves node by node. Choose the Bezier tool. Click to place a corner node (a cusp), or drag to place a smooth node and pull out its handles, which set the direction and the bend of the curve. Go on placing nodes. Double-click or press Enter to finish. To close the curve, click its first node. Esc throws away the curve you are drawing. Hold Ctrl to place the next node in steps of 15 degrees from the last one, or to turn a handle in such steps. Every node snaps to what snapping is set to; see Snapping. Pen The Pen tool places nodes the same way as the Bezier tool: click for a corner node, drag for a smooth node, double-click or Enter to finish, click the first node to close. While the button is down, the handle follows the pointer, so you see the curve take shape. B-Spline The B-Spline tool draws smooth curves from control points, without handles. Click to place each control point. The curve follows the points, starting at the first and ending at the last, and always stays inside them. While you draw, the control points show as a dashed line. Double-click or press Enter to finish. Click the first point (once there are three) to close the curve into a smooth loop. The result is an ordinary curve; the control points are not kept. Polyline The Polyline tool draws straight segments one after the other: click to add each corner, and double-click or press Enter to finish. Hold Ctrl to keep each segment to steps of 15 degrees. 3-Point Curve The 3-Point Curve tool draws an arc through three points: Drag from where the curve starts to where it ends. Hold Ctrl to keep this line to steps of 15 degrees, for a level arc. Move the pointer to bend the curve, and click the point it passes through. Hold Ctrl for a bow, a part of a circle that stands evenly on the line. Continuing a curve To add to an open curve, select it, then draw with the Freehand, 2-Point Line, Bezier, Pen, B-Spline or Polyline tool starting (or ending) on one of its end nodes. The new line becomes part of the curve: it runs on from that end; when it ends on the curve's other end, the curve closes; when it ends on an end of another part of the same curve, the two parts join. The pointer shows a node with a line going on from it when you are over an end node, and a ring when a click would close the curve. The curve keeps its look and stays selected, and the change is one undo step. Closed curves, several selected objects and objects inside groups are never continued. The distance that counts as "on the node" is set on the Curve tools page of the tool options; see Tool options. The property bar While a curve tool is active, the property bar shows the position, size, scale, angle and mirror buttons of the selection, its outline width, line style and start and end arrowheads, and a button that closes an open curve. The Freehand tool adds the smoothing. With nothing selected, it reminds you how to finish a curve. See Outlines for the outline settings. Editing curves afterwards Use the Shape tool to move, add and delete nodes, change their type and bend segments; see Shaping curves with the Shape tool.

h: Brush Strokes Modes Settings Painterly Brush Brushes and settings
x: Brush strokes and painterly brushes Brush strokes turn a line you draw into a filled shape with a varying width, like ink from a pen or a brush. Painterly brushes paint the outline of an object with marks of chalk, ink, watercolor and other media. Brush Strokes The Brush Strokes tool (I) draws strokes in one of five modes. The stroke is a filled object: it takes the current fill color (black when there is none) and no outline, and you edit it like any curve. To draw a brush stroke: Choose the Brush Strokes tool. Choose a mode and its settings on the property bar or in the Brush Strokes panel. Drag on the page. To turn existing curves into strokes, select them and click Apply to curve in the Brush Strokes panel.  Modes Calligraphic: a flat nib of the given width, held at the given angle (45 degrees at first). The stroke is thinnest where you move along the nib and widest across it. Preset: a stroke whose width follows a profile: taper both ends (at first), taper start, taper end, bulge, wave or flat. The width is the widest point. Brush: a preset profile with a rough, dry-brush edge. Expression: the width follows your speed as if it were pen pressure: slow strokes are wide. The pressure setting scales the effect. Sprayer: shapes (circles, squares, stars, hearts or leaves) placed along the line every spacing (8 mm at first), each between 70% and 100% of the width. Settings Width: 3 mm at first. Angle: the nib's angle, for Calligraphic. Smoothing: 0 to 100 (25 at first). Higher values smooth out wobbles. Pressure: for Expression (0.5 at first). Spacing: for Sprayer. Painterly Brush The Painterly Brush tool, in the same flyout, paints a line made of brush marks. The brushstroke is an ordinary curve with no fill: the Shape tool reshapes it, the outline color colors it, and the marks follow. To paint a stroke: Choose the Painterly Brush tool. Choose a brush, a size and a transparency on the property bar. Drag on the page. To paint the outline of existing objects, click them to select them, then pick a brush: their outlines are painted with it. Changing the size or the transparency changes their brushstrokes. Clear Brushstroke gives the selected objects their plain outline back. Brushes and settings Brush: dry media (Chalk, which is the first, Charcoal, Soft Pastel), wet media (Ink Wash, Watercolour, Dry Brush) and textures (Bristle, Fur, Spray, Speckle, Cloud, Silk Ribbon). Brush size: 0.1 to 200 mm, 5 mm at first. Transparency: 0 to 100%, 20% at first. Most brushes thin out towards both ends. The marks are laid the same way each time the stroke is drawn, exported or printed. With "Scale with object" on, the marks grow and shrink with the object. In SVG and PDF exports the marks become filled shapes with their transparency.

h: Shape Recognition Sketch
x: Sketching and shape recognition Two tools turn quick hand-drawn strokes into clean objects: the Shape Recognition tool recognizes the shape you meant, and the Sketch tool builds a smooth line from several strokes. Shape Recognition The Shape Recognition tool (Shift+S) turns a freehand stroke into the shape it looks like, as you drew it: a tilted rectangle stays tilted. Choose the Shape Recognition tool. Draw the shape in one stroke. A stroke whose ends come close together is taken as closed. Release the button. What you get: An open stroke that is nearly straight becomes a straight line; otherwise a smooth curve. A closed stroke with four corners near right angles becomes a rectangle. When it is nearly level, it comes out level. A closed, rounded stroke becomes an ellipse, level when nearly level and never tilted when nearly round. A closed stroke with three corners becomes a triangle, and one with four other corners a four-sided shape. Anything else becomes a smooth closed curve. The new object takes the default fill and outline and is selected. On the property bar, Shape recognition sets how readily strokes become shapes, and Smoothing how much the leftover curves are smoothed. Each is None, Lowest, Low, Medium (at first), High or Highest. With recognition at None, every stroke stays a curve. Sketch The Sketch tool (S) lets you build a line from several short strokes, as you would with a pencil. Choose the Sketch tool. Draw a stroke. It is smoothed and selected. Draw the next stroke starting near the end of the first. With Join on, it is added to the same curve. On the property bar, Join adds a stroke to the selected open curve when it starts close enough to its end; the distance beside it sets how close (5 mm at first). Smoothing sets how much each stroke is smoothed, from None to Highest.

h: Drawing with a box Rectangle Corners 3-Point Rectangle Ellipse 3-Point Ellipse The Corners panel
x: Drawing rectangles and ellipses Rectangles and ellipses stay rectangles and ellipses after you draw them: you can change their corners, turn an ellipse into a pie or an arc, and still resize them freely. To edit them node by node, convert them to curves with Object > Convert to Curves. Drawing with a box The Rectangle, Ellipse, polygon, star, spiral, graph paper, common shapes and action lines tools all draw by dragging a box. While you drag, the object itself follows the pointer, with the settings of the property bar. Hold Ctrl to draw a square, a circle or a regular shape. Hold Shift to draw from the center out. You can press or release it while dragging. The start and end points snap to what snapping is set to. The new object takes the default fill and outline (no fill and a thin black outline at first) and is selected. To change those defaults, see Object styles and defaults. Rectangle Choose the Rectangle tool (F6) and drag from one corner to the opposite one. Double-click the tool's button to draw a rectangle the size of the page; hold Shift while you double-click to frame the selection instead. Corners The property bar sets the corners of the selected rectangles, or of new ones when nothing is selected: The corner style: Round (a quarter circle), Scalloped (a quarter circle cut inwards) or Chamfered (a straight cut). The four sizes: top left, top right, bottom left and bottom right. The size is the radius, or for a chamfer how far from the corner the cut starts. A corner is at most half the shorter side. Edit corners together (the lock, on at first) gives all four the size you type in one. Relative corner scaling (on at first): the corners grow and shrink with the rectangle. Turned off, they keep their size when you resize the rectangle and stay round when you stretch it. You can also drag a corner node with the Shape tool to round all corners at once. 3-Point Rectangle The 3-Point Rectangle tool draws a rectangle at an angle: Drag to draw the base line, at any angle (hold Ctrl for steps of 15 degrees). Move the pointer to set the height and click. Ellipse Choose the Ellipse tool (F7) and drag a box. Hold Ctrl for a circle. On the property bar, choose Ellipse, Pie or Arc. For a pie or an arc, set the start and end angles (in degrees, counterclockwise from the right) and the direction. You can also drag the node of an ellipse with the Shape tool to make a pie (drag inside) or an arc (drag outside). 3-Point Ellipse The 3-Point Ellipse tool draws an ellipse at an angle: Drag to draw the center line of the ellipse, at any angle (hold Ctrl for steps of 15 degrees). Move the pointer to set the height and click. The Corners panel The Corners panel rounds, scallops or chamfers the corners of curves, which the rectangle settings cannot do. Open it from Window > Panels.  Select one or more objects. Rectangles, ellipses, polygons and text become curves when the corners are cut. Choose the Operation: Fillet (a round arc that touches both sides), Scallop (a notch, a quarter of a circle around the corner) or Chamfer (a straight cut). Set the Radius for a fillet or scallop (2 mm at first), or the Chamfer distance for a chamfer: the first distance along the side the path comes in on and the second along the side it leaves on. Equal distances keeps them the same. The result shows as a dashed outline on the drawing. Click Apply. A corner is a node where two segments meet at an angle; smooth nodes are not corners. With the Shape tool and some nodes selected, only those corners are cut. A corner whose sides are too short for the cut is skipped.

t: Drawing polygons, stars, spirals and other shapes
h: Polygon Star Spiral Common Shapes Action Lines Graph Paper
x: Drawing polygons, stars, spirals and other shapes These tools draw ready-made shapes by dragging a box. As with rectangles, hold Ctrl to keep the shape regular and Shift to draw from the center; see Drawing with a box. Polygon The Polygon tool (Y) draws a regular polygon. Set the number of points (3 to 500, 5 at first) on the property bar before or after drawing. The first corner is at the top center. Polygons are symmetric: when you move one node with the Shape tool, the matching nodes of every side move with it, so you can turn a pentagon into a flower in one drag. Star The Star tool draws a star. Its property bar starts with two buttons that choose what it draws: Star: a star with the given number of points (5 at first) and sharpness (0.5 at first; 0 makes a polygon, 1 the thinnest spikes). Complex star: a star whose sides cross, made by joining each point to one further on (9 points and sharpness 2 at first). Its middle stays empty. With some numbers of points it is made of several closed shapes, as six points give two triangles. Spiral The Spiral tool (A) draws a spiral, an open curve. On the property bar set the revolutions (1 to 100, 4 at first) and choose a symmetrical spiral, whose turns are evenly spaced, or a logarithmic one, whose turns grow further apart. Hold Ctrl to draw a round spiral. Common Shapes The Common Shapes tool draws ready-made shapes. Click the shape button on the property bar to choose one from five sets: Basic shapes: parallelogram, trapezoid, diamond, triangles, hexagon, octagon, plus, heart, lightning, crescent, ring, cylinder, cube, frame, teardrop, smiley face and no symbol. Arrows: in every direction, chevron, pentagon, notched, striped and bent arrows. Flowchart: process, decision, data, document, terminator, connector, storage and the other usual symbols. Banners: ribbons, waves, scroll, explosion, burst and pennant. Callouts: rectangle, rounded, oval, cloud and line callouts. Then drag a box. The shape becomes one curve with the default fill and outline. Parts that should look separate, such as the faces of a cube, are separate parts of the curve, and holes such as the middle of a ring stay holes whatever the fill. Action Lines The Action Lines tool draws speed lines in a comic-book style: a group of lines (2 to 500, 12 at first) that are parallel (at first) or radial. Their lengths vary, but the same box always gives the same lines. Graph Paper The Graph Paper tool (D) draws a grid of cells: a group of rectangles that fill the box exactly. Set the rows and columns (4 by 3 at first) on the property bar. Hold Ctrl for square cells. The default points, revolutions, rows and columns are also on the tool pages of the options; see Tool options.

t: Shaping curves with the Shape tool
h: Nodes and segments Selecting nodes Moving nodes and bending segments The property bar Aligning nodes Rectangles, ellipses, polygons and other objects
x: Shaping curves with the Shape tool The Shape tool (F10) edits the nodes and segments of a curve: you move nodes, bend segments, add and delete nodes and change how each node joins its segments. Nodes and segments Select a curve with the Shape tool. Its outline shows in the node color, its nodes as small markers, and the first node of each part of the curve as a slightly larger triangle. A selected node shows its control handles: dashed lines that end in an arrow at the control point. A node is one of three types: Cusp: the segments meet at an angle; each handle moves on its own. Smooth: the curve passes through without a corner; the two handles stay in line. Symmetrical: smooth, with both handles the same length. The pointer shows what a press would take: a small square over a node, a dot over a control handle, a wave over a segment. Selecting nodes Click a node to select it alone; Ctrl+click adds it or takes it out of the selection. Shift+click selects every node from the last selected one to the one you click. Drag a marquee around nodes. The property bar's selection mode chooses a rectangular or a freehand marquee. Tab and Shift+Tab select the next or previous node; Home and End the first or last. Ctrl+A, the select all nodes button, or a double-click on the tool's button selects every node. Moving nodes and bending segments Drag a node to move the selected nodes. Hold Ctrl to move only horizontally or vertically. Nodes snap like drawing points. Drag a segment to bend it: the point you grab follows the pointer while the nodes at its ends stay. A straight segment becomes curved. Drag a control handle to change the bend. The arrow keys nudge the selected nodes (Shift for a larger step, Ctrl for a smaller one). Double-click a segment to add a node there, a node to delete it. Click a segment to mark a spot, then press + to add a node there. Delete or - deletes the selected nodes; + adds a node in the middle of each segment that ends at them. With nodes selected, C switches them between cusp and smooth, S between smooth and symmetrical, and Y makes them symmetrical. With nodes selected, Ctrl+C copies the segments between them as new curves, Ctrl+X cuts them out, and Ctrl+D duplicates them. Right-click a node or segment for a menu of the commands below. The property bar Selection mode: rectangular or freehand marquee. Add node and Delete node. Join nodes joins two end nodes into one; Break curve splits the curve at the selected node. Convert to line and Convert to curve make the segment ending at the node straight or curved. Cusp, Smooth and Symmetrical set the node type. Reverse direction turns the curve round; Extend curve to close joins two selected end nodes with a straight segment; Extract subpath makes the part of the selected node a curve of its own; Close curve closes an open curve. Stretch and scale nodes and Rotate and skew nodes frame two or more selected nodes with handles: the corner handles scale (or rotate), the side handles stretch (or skew) only those nodes. Align nodes opens the Node Align dialog box (see below). Reflect horizontally and Reflect vertically: moving a node moves the selected nodes on the other side the mirrored way, so both sides of a shape change together. Elastic mode: the selected nodes move less the further they are from the one you drag, down to half as much for the furthest. Select all nodes. Reduce nodes removes nodes that are not needed, from the selected nodes or from the whole curve. Drag the curve smoothness slider to remove more nodes gradually. Aligning nodes To line up nodes: Select two or more nodes with the Shape tool. Click Align nodes on the property bar. In the Node Align dialog box, tick Align horizontal, Align vertical or both, and click OK. The selected nodes move onto a common horizontal or vertical line, or onto one point when both are ticked. The align keys work on the selected nodes too, two or more: L and R line them up with the leftmost or rightmost node, T and B with the top or bottom node, and E puts them on the middle of their height. Their control handles move with them. (C keeps making a node cusp here.)  Rectangles, ellipses, polygons and other objects Drag a corner node of a rectangle to round every corner; Ctrl+drag (or click it first) to round that corner only. Drag the node of an ellipse inside it to make a pie, outside it to make an arc. Drag a node of a polygon or star: the matching nodes follow, so the shape stays symmetric. Dragging the points between the corners sharpens or twists a star. Double-click a rectangle, ellipse or polygon to turn it into a curve. Drag a corner of a picture to crop it: the picture goes into a frame whose nodes you can edit like a curve. With text, the Shape tool moves single characters; see Adding and editing text. The appearance of nodes and handles is set on the Nodes and Handles page of the options; see TraceDraw options.

h: Using a shaping brush Smooth Smear Twirl Attract and Repel Smudge Roughen
x: Smoothing, smearing and roughening outlines The shaping brushes of the Shape flyout reshape the outline of an object where you drag over it, like a sculptor's tool: Smooth, Smear, Twirl, Attract and Repel, Smudge and Roughen. Using a shaping brush Select a curve. Other objects are converted to curves first; with nothing selected, the object under the pointer is used. Choose the tool and set its Nib size (the radius of the brush, 10 mm at first) and its other settings on the property bar. Drag over the outline. The effect is strongest at the center of the nib and fades to nothing at its edge. Only the parts of the outline within reach change; open curves stay open and closed ones stay closed. Each drag is one undo step. The settings are kept for the next time. Smooth The Smooth tool removes wobbles and extra nodes where you drag. Rate (1 to 100%, 20% at first) sets how strongly. Smear The Smear tool (W) pulls the outline along with the pointer, as if you smeared wet paint. Pressure (1 to 100%, 100% at first) sets how far it moves. Twirl The Twirl tool turns the outline around the pointer into a swirl. Speed (1 to 100%, 50% at first) sets how fast it turns, and the direction buttons choose counterclockwise or clockwise; hold Alt or Shift while dragging to turn the other way. Holding the pointer still keeps turning. Attract and Repel The Attract and Repel tool pulls the nodes inside the nib towards the pointer, or pushes them away. Speed (1 to 100%, 50% at first) sets how fast; choose Attract or Repel on the property bar, or hold Alt or Shift while dragging to swap them. Holding the pointer still keeps going. Smudge The Smudge tool (V) smooths the outline slightly, then smears it, so it is pulled without kinks. Pressure (1 to 100%, 100% at first) sets how far. Roughen The Roughen tool (E) adds jagged spikes along the outline. Frequency (1 to 10 spikes per 10 mm, 5 at first) sets how many, and Spike size (2 mm at first) how tall. The spikes are straight, so they stay sharp.

h: Crop Knife Segment Delete Eraser
x: Cropping, cutting and erasing Four tools of the Crop flyout take parts of objects away: Crop, Knife, Segment Delete and Eraser. Each change is one undo step. Crop The Crop tool removes everything outside a rectangle. Select the objects to crop, or select nothing to crop every unlocked object on the page. Choose the Crop tool and drag the crop area. The drawing outside it is dimmed. Adjust the area: drag inside it to move it, drag one of its eight handles to resize it, or type its position and size on the property bar. Double-click inside the area, press Enter or click Crop on the property bar. To give up, press Esc, click outside the area, click Clear crop area, or choose another tool. What happens to each object: objects wholly inside stay as they are, and objects wholly outside are deleted; closed shapes are cut to the area, and open curves are cut where they cross its edge; text becomes curves first; bitmaps, tables and symbols are placed inside a frame of the area, so their content stays whole and can be taken out again (see Clip frames); groups are cropped member by member. Knife The Knife tool splits objects along a cut. Select the objects to cut, or select nothing to cut every visible object on the page. Choose the Knife tool and the kind of cut on the property bar: Two-point line (a straight cut that runs on across the objects) or Freehand (a cut that follows your drag). Drag across the objects. On the property bar, Split separates the pieces with a hairline gap, so they still meet, and Gap removes a band of the width you type. With Keep as one object, the pieces of each object stay one object made of several parts. Open curves are split where the cut crosses them. Pieces keep the fill, outline and transparency and are selected. Bitmaps, groups and text are not cut. Segment Delete The Segment Delete tool deletes the parts of outlines between the places where they cross other outlines or themselves, for example the bits of lines that stick out past a crossing. Click a part of an outline to delete it. Drag a rectangle across outlines to delete every part it touches, on all objects at once. Each part goes whole, up to the crossings at its ends, even where it reaches past the rectangle; a closed shape that nothing crosses goes whole. Rectangles, ellipses and polygons become curves; a closed shape that loses a part opens, and an object with nothing left is deleted. Eraser The Eraser tool (X) rubs out parts of objects. Select the objects to erase, or select nothing to erase the object you start dragging on. Choose the Eraser tool. Set the thickness (6.35 mm at first) and the round or square nib on the property bar. Drag over the objects. A click erases one dot. Erased objects become curves; an object erased completely is deleted. Double-click an object with the tool to delete it whole. Bitmaps, groups and clip frames are not erased. The defaults of the eraser are on the Eraser page of the tool options; see Tool options.

t: Combining shapes: weld, trim and intersect
h: The target and the sources The operations The Shaping panel
x: Combining shapes: weld, trim and intersect Shaping builds new shapes from overlapping objects: join them into one, cut one with another, or keep only where they overlap. The commands are in Object > Shaping, on the property bar when two or more objects are selected, and in the Shaping panel. The target and the sources The last object you select is the target: it gives the result its fill, outline and transparency. The other selected objects are the sources. To choose the target, select the sources first, then Shift+click the target. The result goes on top of the active layer and is selected. Each operation is one undo step. When there is no result (for example two objects that do not overlap), nothing changes and the status bar says so. The operations Weld 2 objects one object covering all of them Trim 2 objects the target without what the sources cover Intersect 2 objects only the area all of them share Simplify 1 object each object without what the objects above it cover Front Minus Back 2 objects the front object without the ones behind it Back Minus Front 2 objects the back object without the ones in front of it Boundary 1 object an outline around the whole selection From the menu and the property bar, Weld removes the originals, Trim keeps the sources, Intersect keeps all of them, and Boundary keeps them all. The Shaping panel Open the Shaping panel from Object > Shaping > Shaping.  Click one of the seven picture buttons to choose the operation. The panel shows its name, a picture and what it does. For Weld, Trim and Intersect, choose what to keep: Leave original source object and Leave original target object. Each operation remembers its own choice. Select the objects, the target last. Click the button named after the operation. It stays pale until enough objects are selected, and a line says how many are needed. Related: Combine (Ctrl+L) makes several objects one curve without changing their shapes, and Break Apart splits a curve into its parts again. See Objects and layers.

h: To join curves
x: Joining curves The Join Curves panel closes the gaps between the ends of curves, for example lines that should meet at a corner but stop short of it. Open it with Object > Join Curves.  To join curves Select the curves. Open parts inside one curve are joined too. Choose how the ends are joined: Extend: both ends carry on in their directions until they meet, as a corner. When the directions never meet ahead of both ends, a straight line joins them. Chamfer: a straight line between the ends. Fillet: as Extend, then the corner is rounded with the radius (2 mm at first). Bezier curve: a smooth curve that leaves and arrives in the directions of the ends. Set the gap tolerance (5 mm at first). Ends further apart are not joined. Click Apply. The closest pair of ends is joined first, then the next, until no pair is left within the tolerance; the two ends of one part close it. The joined curve takes the place, fill and outline of the curve you selected last, and the other curves are removed. When no ends lie close enough, nothing changes and the status bar says so. You can also join two end nodes of one curve with the Shape tool; see Shaping curves with the Shape tool. Drawing from the end of a selected curve also continues it; see Continuing a curve.

h: Opening the outline settings Outline Pen settings Outline Color Variable Outline
x: Setting outlines The outline is the line drawn along the edge of an object. You set its color, width, style, corners, line ends and arrowheads in the Outline section of the Properties panel. Opening the outline settings The Outline Pen tool (F12) opens the Outline Pen dialog box with every outline setting: color, width and its unit, style, miter limit, dashes, corners, line caps, position, arrowheads, calligraphy, Behind fill, Scale with object, the variable outline's width nodes and Overprint outline. OK changes only what you changed, on every selected object; with nothing selected it sets the outline of new objects.  Double-click the outline part of the status bar. Right-click a color of the palette to color the outline of the selection. Outline Pen settings Width: 0.2 mm for new objects. Hairline draws a line one screen or printer dot wide at every zoom. Paint: the outline can be painted like a fill: none, uniform color, gradient, pattern, texture or mesh. See Fills. Hairlines and arrowheads keep the plain outline color. Caps, the ends of open lines: Butt (at first), Round or Square. Corners: Miter (at first), Round or Bevel. Dash: Solid, Dashed, Dotted or Dash dot. The dashes grow with the width. Arrowheads, at the Start and the End of open lines, filled in the outline color. To make your own, draw it, select it and choose Object > Create > Arrowhead. The nib stretch (0.1 to 1) and nib angle make a calligraphic outline: thinner across the nib than along it, like a flat pen. Behind fill draws the outline under the fill, so only its outer half shows. Scale with object: the width grows and shrinks when you resize the object. To turn an outline into an object you can fill, choose Object > Convert Outline to Object (Ctrl+Shift+Q). The settings of new objects are explained in Object styles and defaults. Outline Color The Outline Color tool (Shift+F12) opens the Color panel to choose the outline color of the selection. See The Color panel. Variable Outline The Variable Outline tool, in the Shape flyout, makes an outline thicker or thinner along its length with width nodes. Select an object with an outline, such as a curve, a rectangle or an ellipse. An object with no outline gets a thin one. Choose the Variable Outline tool. Drag across the outline: a width node is added where you start, and the outline reaches to the pointer on both sides. Hold Shift (or Alt) as you start dragging to change only the side the pointer is on. Shift+click picks a run of nodes and Ctrl+click adds one; a drag then changes all the picked nodes. Add more nodes the same way. Between nodes the width changes smoothly. To change a node, click it and type the Left width and Right width on the property bar (left is to the left of the path's direction). Delete node or Delete removes the selected node, and Clear variable outline gives back the plain outline.

h: Placing a dimension Parallel Horizontal or Vertical Angular Segment Dimension style Callout
x: Dimension lines and callouts Dimension lines show the size of things in a technical drawing: a length, a horizontal or vertical distance, an angle or the length of a segment. Callouts point at something with a leader line and a label. Both stay live: when you move, scale or turn them, they are measured and drawn again. Placing a dimension Every dimension is placed in clicks, and the property bar says what to click next. While the last point is wanted, the dimension follows the pointer. Esc starts again. Points snap as drawing does, so snapping to nodes or objects gives exact measures; see Snapping. The new dimension is selected. Parallel The Parallel Dimension tool measures the straight distance between two points, at any angle: Drag from the first point to the second, or click both. Move the pointer and click where the dimension line goes. Horizontal or Vertical The Horizontal or Vertical Dimension tool measures only the horizontal or the vertical distance between two points, whichever is larger. Place it as a parallel dimension. Angular The Angular Dimension tool measures an angle: Click the vertex of the angle. Click a point on the first side, then a point on the second side. Click where the arc goes. The angle is measured counterclockwise from the first side. Segment The Segment Dimension tool measures a segment of an object: click the segment to take its two ends, then click where the dimension line goes. Dimension style The property bar shows these settings with the dimension tools and when the selection is all dimensions. Changes apply to the selected dimensions and to the next ones you make. Precision: 0 to 6 decimals (2 at first). Units: the drawing units (at first) or any other unit. Lengths follow the drawing scale, so at 1:100 a 10 mm line reads 1000 mm; see Document options. Show units: the unit after the number (the degree sign for angles). Prefix and Suffix: text before and after the number. Text: above the line (at first), in the line, or below the line. Label size: 1 to 500 points (10 at first). The label always reads left to right and stays upright. Callout The 3-Point Callout tool draws a label with a leader line in two segments. Drag from the tip (what the callout points at) to the elbow, or click both. Click where the text goes. The text goes on that side of the elbow. Type the text. The sample text is selected, so typing replaces it. The leader always ends at the text: when you type more, change the size or move the text on its own (Ctrl+click it), the leader follows. Move the tip or the elbow with the Shape tool. The property bar, shown with the tool and when the selection is all callouts, sets: the outline width of the leader and shape (a hairline at first); the line style; the head at the tip (an arrow at first, or none); the callout shape around the text: none (at first), underline, rectangle, rounded rectangle or ellipse; the gap between the text and the leader or shape (1 mm at first).

h: Anchors Drawing a connector Connector settings Staying attached Editing anchors
x: Connector lines and anchors Connector lines join two objects and stay attached to them: when you move or resize the objects, the connector follows. They are useful for diagrams, flowcharts and organization charts. Anchors A connector attaches to an anchor of each object. Every object has four anchors, at the middle of each side of its bounding box. You can add your own anchors with the Edit Anchor tool; they move and scale with the object. Drawing a connector Three tools in the Connector flyout draw connectors: Straight-Line Connector: a straight line; Right-Angle Connector: horizontal and vertical segments with square corners; Rounded Right-Angle Connector: the same with rounded corners. To join two objects: Choose a connector tool. Drag from one object to the other. While you drag, the anchors of both objects show, and the line starts at the anchor that will be used. Release on the other object. When you start or end the drag on an anchor, that anchor is used; otherwise the closest pair of anchors of the two objects is used. The connector is an open line with no fill and the default outline. Connector settings The property bar, shown with the connector tools and when the selection is all connectors, has the three kinds of connector (with connectors selected, they change how those run), the corner radius of rounded connectors (3 mm at first), and the outline width, style and arrowheads of the selected connectors. Staying attached When you move, scale or reshape the joined objects, the connector runs again between their anchors. When you move the connector together with its objects, it stays attached. When you move the connector on its own, it lets go and becomes a plain line. Undo attaches it again. When one of its objects is deleted, the connector stays where it is. Editing anchors The Edit Anchor tool adds, moves and deletes anchors: Choose the Edit Anchor tool and click an object. Its anchors show as diamonds. Click inside the object to add an anchor there. Drag an anchor you added to move it. Select an anchor and press Delete, double-click it, or click Delete anchor on the property bar to remove it. Remove all custom anchors removes every anchor you added. The four anchors at the middle of the sides cannot be removed.
对象、符号和图层 绘图中的每个形状、线条、文本和图片都是对象。这些页面介绍如何选择对象，移动、调整大小、旋转和对齐它们，如何排列顺序、组合以及用图层组织它们，以及如何把它们作为符号重复使用。 这些页面还介绍有特殊用途的对象：表格、条形码和二维码、注释以及附加到对象的数据。

h: The Pick tool Moving, resizing and turning Dragging with the right button The property bar Selection groups The Freehand Pick tool
x: Selecting objects Before you change an object, you select it. The Pick tool (Space switches to it from most tools) selects, moves and resizes objects; the Freehand Pick tool does the same but selects with a freehand loop. The Pick tool Click an object to select it. A filled object counts where it is filled; an unfilled one on its outline. Text, groups, tables and pictures count anywhere inside their box. Shift+click adds an object to the selection or takes it out. Drag around objects, starting on an empty spot: the objects wholly inside the dashed frame are selected. Hold Alt as you finish the drag to select every object the frame touches. Hold Shift to turn over the objects the frame takes: those selected are deselected and the others added. Hold Ctrl to keep the frame square. Ctrl+click selects an object inside a group, one level further in at each click. Its handles are round, and changes act on it alone. Alt+click selects the object beneath the selected one, to reach objects that are covered. Tab and Shift+Tab select the next or previous object. Esc selects nothing. Edit > Select All and a double-click on the tool's button select every object; Select All also selects all text, guidelines or nodes. The selected objects show eight square handles around them and a small cross in the middle. The status bar says what is selected and on which layer. Moving, resizing and turning Drag a selected object, or the cross in its middle, to move it. Hold Ctrl to move only horizontally or vertically. The object snaps to what snapping is set to. Drag a corner handle to resize in proportion, a side handle to stretch in one direction. Hold Shift to resize from the center, Ctrl to resize in steps of 100% (crossing the other side mirrors the object), Alt to resize freely. Click a selected object again to show the rotation handles: drag a curved corner arrow to rotate, a side arrow to skew. Hold Ctrl for steps of 15 degrees. Drag the ring in the middle to turn about another point; double-click it to put it back in the middle. While dragging, press Space or click the right button to leave a copy where the objects were; Esc cancels the drag. The arrow keys nudge the selection by the nudge distance (2.54 mm at first), with Shift by the super nudge distance and with Ctrl by the micro nudge distance. Set them on the Rulers page of the document options. + duplicates the selection in place. Dragging with the right button Drag a selected object with the right mouse button. When you release, a menu offers to move it there, copy it there, copy its fill, outline or all its properties to the object under the pointer, or place it inside that object as a clip frame. The property bar With nothing selected, the property bar shows the page size and orientation, the drawing units and the nudge distance. With a selection, it shows the position (X and Y), the size (W and H), the scale, the rotation angle, the mirror buttons, the outline width, to front and to back, and convert to curves. Text adds the text settings, and bitmaps the bitmap commands. With several objects, a group or a curve of several parts, it adds group, ungroup, combine, break apart, the shaping commands and the Align and Distribute panel. Selection groups Press Ctrl and a number from 0 to 9 to remember the selection under that number. Press the number alone to select those objects again, and again to zoom to them. Alt and the number add the selection to the group. Groups are saved with the drawing. The Freehand Pick tool The Freehand Pick tool works like the Pick tool, but a drag from an empty spot draws a loop. When you release, every object wholly inside the loop is selected; hold Alt as you release to select every object the loop touches, Shift to add to the selection. Hold Ctrl to draw a rectangle instead. The options of the Pick tool, such as whether a frame selects the objects it touches, are on the Pick page of the tool options; see Tool options.

h: The Transformations panel Position Rotate Scale and Mirror Size Skew The Free Transform tool Undoing transformations The Coordinates panel
x: Moving, scaling, rotating and skewing You can transform objects by dragging them with the Pick tool (see Selecting objects), by typing values on the property bar, with the Free Transform tool, or precisely with the Transformations panel. The Transformations panel Open the panel with Object > Transformations, or with Alt+F7 (Position), Alt+F8 (Rotate), Alt+F9 (Scale and Mirror) and Alt+F10 (Size). The buttons at the top choose one of five pages.  Every page ends with the reference point, a 3 by 3 grid that chooses the point of the selection that is placed, turned about or kept still (the center at first), Copies and Apply. Distances are in the drawing units, angles in degrees (counterclockwise), scales in percent. To transform the selection: Choose a page and type the values. Choose the reference point. Set Copies: 0 changes the selection itself; a number above 0 leaves the selection as it is and adds that many copies, each transformed once more than the one before. The copies are one undo step, and the last copy becomes the selection, so another Apply goes on from there. Click Apply. Position X and Y move the selection. With Relative position on (at first), they are a distance to move by; off, they are where the reference point goes, counted from the ruler origin. With Relative position on, the grid picks a direction: a side or a corner sets the distance to the selection's size, so each copy lands right next to the last one. Rotate Type the angle, and the Center to turn about. With Relative center on (at first), the center is counted from the reference point; off, from the ruler origin. Scale and Mirror X and Y scale in percent (100% at first). Mirror horizontally and Mirror vertically flip the selection. Proportional keeps both scales the same. Size W and H set the width and height of the selection. Proportional keeps the proportions. Skew X and Y slant the selection by angles. With Use anchor point on, the reference point stays still; off, the center does. The Free Transform tool The Free Transform tool, in the Pick flyout, transforms the selection about the point where you press. Choose a mode on the property bar: Free rotation (at first): turns the selection around the press point. Free angle reflection: mirrors the selection across the line from the press point to the pointer; moving the pointer turns that line. Free scale: scales about the press point. Free skew: horizontal movement skews horizontally, vertical movement vertically. Hold Alt to scale, Ctrl to skew or Shift to reflect for one drag, whatever the mode. With Apply to duplicate on, the press makes a copy and the drag transforms the copy, leaving the original as it was. The property bar also has the position, size, scale, angle and mirror fields. Undoing transformations Object > Clear Transformations takes the selected objects back to how they were before they were scaled, rotated or skewed. The Coordinates panel The Coordinates panel draws an object from typed coordinates, or reshapes the selected one, with a dashed preview on the drawing. Open it from Window > Panels.  Choose the kind of object with the buttons at the top: rectangle or square, ellipse or circle, polygon or regular polygon, star, complex star, 2-point line or multipoint curve. Type its values: rectangles and ellipses: the position of the origin point (chosen in a 3 by 3 grid), the width and height, the angle of rotation, and the corners of the bounding box while the angle is 0; squares and circles: the position, the side or diameter and the angle; polygons and stars: the number of points or sides, the sharpness, the angle and the circle the points lie on; regular polygons: the number of sides, the length of a side, the angle and the center; 2-point lines: the start point and end point, or the length and angle; multipoint curves: the list of points, with buttons to add and delete points and to close the curve. Instead of typing, click a button with a pointer and target, then click or drag on the drawing to set that value. A right click cancels. Click Create object to add it, or Replace object to reshape the selected rectangle, ellipse, polygon or curve while keeping its fill, outline, name and place. Positions are counted from the ruler origin, in the drawing units.

h: Aligning Distributing Fit objects to a path
x: Aligning and distributing objects Aligning lines objects up by their edges or centers; distributing spaces them evenly. Use the Align and Distribute panel (Ctrl+Shift+A), the commands of Object > Align and Distribute, or the keys below.  Aligning Select the objects. Select the one the others should line up with last. In the Align part of the panel, choose Align to: Active object (at first): the object selected last; with one object selected, the page; Page edge: the edges of the page; Page center: the center of the page; Grid: each object to the nearest line of the document grid. Click one of the six buttons: left edges, centers on a vertical line, right edges, top edges, centers on a horizontal line, or bottom edges. Use outline: align the outer edges of the outlines: with this on, the outer edges of the outlines meet, instead of the paths themselves. The keys always align to the object selected last: L Align Left R Align Right T Align Top B Align Bottom E Align Centers Horizontally C Align Centers Vertically P Center to Page Distributing Select three or more objects (two or more to distribute across the page). In the Distribute part, choose Distribute to: Selection extent (at first): the first and last objects stay where they are, and the others move between them; Page extent: the objects spread across the whole page, the first touching one side and the last the other. Click one of the eight buttons: left edges, centers, gaps or right edges across the page, or top edges, centers, gaps or bottom edges down it. Spreading the gaps gives equal space between the objects whatever their sizes. With too few objects the buttons are pale and the panel says how many are needed. Each align or distribute is one undo step. To place copies at even distances in one step, see Step and repeat. Fit objects to a path The Fit Objects to Path panel places objects along a line, a curve or the outline of a shape. Open it with Object > Fit Objects to Path. Select the objects to place, then the path last (Shift+click). Under Spacing, choose Evenly along the path to spread the objects over the whole path, or Fixed distance and type the Distance between the centers of neighbouring objects. Start offset moves the first object along the path from its start. Tick Rotate objects to follow the path to turn each object with the direction of the path, and Reverse direction to start from the other end. Once you change a value, the outlines on the canvas show where the objects will go. Click Apply. The panel starts from its default values, with no outlines, each time you select other objects (or work in another drawing); the values you enter stay while the same objects are selected. On a closed shape the objects go all the way round without the first and last meeting. Fitting is one undo step.

t: Making copies with Step and Repeat
h: To make copies
x: Making copies with Step and Repeat The Step and Repeat panel makes several copies of the selection, each moved by the same distance from the one before: a row of buttons, a column of lines, a grid of tiles. Open it with Edit > Step and Repeat (Ctrl+Shift+D).  To make copies Select the objects to copy. Set the number of Number of copies (1 to 999). Under Horizontal settings, choose how the copies are spaced across: Offset: the distance from one copy to the next, measured from the same point of each; Spacing: the gap between one copy and the next, so the copies never overlap whatever their size. Then type the distance. 0 keeps the copies in line. Do the same under Vertical settings. Click Apply. The copies are added to the active layer and selected. Distances are in the drawing units. The values are for the objects selected when they were typed. Selecting other objects, or the copies an Apply just made, puts the number of copies, the distances and the modes back to their defaults, so the next Apply never reuses a count meant for another object. With nothing selected the fields wait at their defaults. To copy with a rotation or a scale at each step, use the Copies field of the Transformations panel; see Moving, scaling, rotating and skewing.

h: The Objects panel Layers Master layers Renaming objects and layers Changing the order Grouping and combining Locking and hiding objects
x: Organizing objects and layers The Objects panel shows how the current page is organized: its layers, the objects on each layer, the groups and the master layers that appear on every page. Use it to select, name, hide, lock and order objects and layers. Objects higher in the list are drawn in front.  The Objects panel The panel lists the page with its layers, topmost first, then the Master Page with the master layers, the guidelines (Guides) and the Document Grid. Each object shows a swatch of its fill framed in its outline color, and its name, or what it is when it has none ("Rectangle", "Curve with 8 nodes"). Click an object to select it; Shift+click adds it to the selection. Its layer becomes the active layer. Click the arrow of a group to see the objects inside it. Each layer has three buttons: Show/hide, Print and export the layer and Lock layer. A hidden or locked layer cannot be edited. The padlock of Guides locks all the guidelines of the page. Hidden objects show their name dimmed. Layers A layer is a sheet on which objects lie. The active layer, shown in bold with a colored bar, is where new objects go when you draw, paste, duplicate or import. Click a layer to make it active. New Layer, at the bottom of the panel, adds a layer on top and makes it active. Right-click a layer for Rename, Move up, Move down and Delete layer. A page always keeps one layer. Delete at the bottom of the panel deletes the selected objects, or the active layer when nothing is selected. Master layers Objects on a master layer appear on every page, under the page's own layers: use them for a logo, a header or page numbers. Click the New Master Layer (All Pages); right-click for odd or even pages button to add one for all pages; right-click it to add one for odd or even pages only. A master layer's menu has Show on to choose All pages, Odd pages or Even pages. You can select and edit master objects from any page they show on. Renaming objects and layers Double-click a layer or an object in the panel, or choose Rename from its menu, to open the Rename Layer or Rename Object dialog box. Type the new name and click OK. An object with an empty name shows what it is again. Double-click the page row to rename the page.  Names help you find objects in the panel and in Find and replace, and are kept in exported SVG files. Changing the order Object > Order moves the selected objects: To Front of Page, To Back of Page, To Front of Layer, To Back of Layer, Forward One, Back One, In Front Of, Behind (click the object to go in front of or behind) and Reverse Order. Grouping and combining Object > Group > Group (Ctrl+G) makes the selection one group that moves and resizes together. Ungroup (Ctrl+U) splits it again, and Ungroup All also splits the groups inside it. To edit an object inside a group without ungrouping, Ctrl+click it. Combine (Ctrl+L) makes the selected objects one curve of several parts, with one fill and outline; where the parts overlap, holes appear. Break Apart (Ctrl+K) splits a curve into its parts. Convert to Curves (Ctrl+Q) turns a rectangle, ellipse, polygon or text into a curve you can edit node by node. Locking and hiding objects Object > Lock > Lock Object keeps the selected objects from being selected or changed; Unlock Object and Unlock All Objects release them. Object > Hide > Hide Object hides the selected objects; Show All Objects shows them again. To keep objects out of the way while you work on others, see also Focus mode.

h: With objects selected With nothing selected
x: The Properties panel The Properties panel (Alt+Enter) shows and changes the properties of the selected objects: their outline, fill, transparency and more, depending on what is selected. It is open at first, beside Hints and Objects. Open it again with Object > Properties.  With objects selected The top of the panel names the selected object (and how many more are selected) and gives its position and size. Under it, a row of buttons opens and closes each section the object has: QR code, for a QR code: its content and look; see Barcodes and QR codes. Outline: color, width, paint, caps, corners, dashes, arrowheads and more; see Setting outlines. Fill: the kind of fill and its settings; see Fills. F11 opens this section. Transparency: how much of what lies below shows through; see Transparency. Rectangle, for rectangles: the corner settings; see Corners. FX: the bitmap effects applied to the object; see Bitmap effects. Character, for text: the font, size, Bold and Italic, and a button to Edit with the Text tool (F8). Summary: a summary of the object. The sections you closed stay closed the next time. A change applies to every selected object and is one undo step. With nothing selected With nothing selected, the panel says No objects selected and shows the Default properties for new objects: the fill and outline that new shapes and lines get.
